subject: maths

moments.title: Bayes's posthumous theorem
moments.who: Thomas Bayes (posthumous), edited by Richard Price
moments.body:
Bayes, a Presbyterian minister and amateur mathematician, dies in 1761. His friend Richard Price discovers an unpublished manuscript: 'An Essay towards solving a Problem in the Doctrine of Chances'.

The paper contains what we now call Bayes's theorem — a rule for updating beliefs given new evidence. Price publishes it in 1763.

Bayes himself probably did not realise the full significance. Laplace develops Bayesian methods more fully decades later.
moments.takeaway: A foundational paper of modern statistics is published posthumously, by a friend.

moments.title: Galton — regression to mediocrity
moments.body:
Francis Galton (Darwin's cousin) studies the heights of fathers and sons. He notices tall fathers tend to have shorter sons (relative to the mean), short fathers taller sons. He calls this 'regression to mediocrity' — later 'regression to the mean'.

Galton coins the term 'regression' for the statistical procedure of fitting lines to data. His work founds biometry — the application of statistics to biology.

He also coined 'eugenics' and was deeply involved in promoting it — a moral stain on his legacy.
moments.takeaway: Regression analysis is born. Its founder's broader social views are now repudiated, but the mathematical contribution endures.

moments.title: Karl Pearson and the chi-squared test
moments.body:
Karl Pearson, Galton's protégé and successor, founds the world's first statistics department at UCL. He develops the chi-squared test (1900), the correlation coefficient, the method of moments, and the journal Biometrika.

Pearson's statistical machinery becomes the standard toolkit of 20th-century biological and social sciences. He is also a vocal eugenicist.
moments.takeaway: Statistical inference becomes systematised. The institutional structure of modern statistics is built.

moments.title: Fisher's Statistical Methods for Research Workers
moments.who: Ronald A. Fisher, Rothamsted Experimental Station
moments.body:
R. A. Fisher publishes 'Statistical Methods for Research Workers' — a textbook that defines modern hypothesis testing, p-values, design of experiments, analysis of variance (ANOVA), and maximum likelihood estimation.

Fisher works on agricultural experiments at Rothamsted (the world's longest-running agricultural research site). His methods for testing fertiliser effects, breeding strategies, etc., become THE methods of empirical science.

Fisher is also a leading eugenicist. His statistical brilliance and his social views are inextricable historically.

quote.text: To call in the statistician after the experiment is done may be no more than asking him to perform a post-mortem examination: he may be able to say what the experiment died of.

moments.takeaway: Modern frequentist statistics is essentially Fisher's invention. His framework dominates 20th-century empirical science.

moments.title: Neyman-Pearson framework and Kolmogorov axioms
moments.who: Jerzy Neyman and Egon Pearson (London), Andrey Kolmogorov (Moscow)
moments.body:
Neyman and Pearson formalise hypothesis testing as a decision between two hypotheses, with calculated probabilities of Type I and Type II errors. This is distinct from Fisher's significance testing — Fisher hated their formalisation.

In the same year, Kolmogorov publishes 'Foundations of the Theory of Probability', putting probability on a measure-theoretic axiomatic foundation. Modern probability theory's mathematical foundation is set.
moments.takeaway: Statistical inference and probability are formalised. Different schools of statistics (Fisher, Neyman-Pearson, Bayesian) coexist.

now.title: Statistics today
now.body:
Statistics is a major discipline of its own. Bayesian methods, revived by computational power (MCMC) since the 1990s, are now mainstream. Machine learning has merged with statistics: gradient boosting, neural networks, deep learning all use statistical foundations.

Applications: clinical trials, epidemiology, economics, sports analytics, finance, A/B testing in tech, gene expression studies, election polling. Every empirical science uses statistics.
now.open_questions: How to communicate uncertainty effectively? How to fix the replication crisis? When to use frequentist vs Bayesian methods? Can causal inference from observational data be trusted? How to deal with high-dimensional data where classical methods fail?

reflection: Galton, Pearson and Fisher — three founders of modern statistics — were all enthusiastic eugenicists. Their statistical methods are sound; their social applications were repugnant. How should a discipline reckon with founders whose mathematics is timeless but whose politics were monstrous? What does this teach us about the relationship between method and value?
